session_name: Technological Change at Work and Across Industries
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Deepa Kylasam Iyer (Cornell University), Ayaj Rana (Cornell University), Adam Seth Litwin (Cornell University)
author_names: Kylasam Iyer*, Deepa; Rana, Ayaj; Litwin, Adam Seth
title: Technology Makers as De Facto Job Designers in American Healthcare
abstract: As the U.S. healthcare system hobbles along, key stakeholders look to technology—these days, artificial intelligence (AI)—to improve sectoral performance. But this performance panacea won't come to fruition if it worsens the psychological strain on clinicians by intensifying their workload and narrowing their discretion. Our analysis shows this is precisely what's occurring. Using qualitative analysis of marketing materials from 100 U.S. healthcare AI technology "makers", i.e., developers, marketers, etc., complemented by 19 trade journal articles quoting hospital administrators, we show how makers act as de facto job designers. Makers converge on four value constellations: efficiency, spreadability, and precision—that translate into design imperatives and, in turn, into three solution archetypes: turnkey, configurable, and customizable. Each archetype implies a distinctive job-design bundle. Turnkey systems elevate demands and limit resources; configurable systems provide bounded flexibility with contingent effects; and customizable systems expand discretion, learning, and feedback. We document a market-level "job-design tilt": makers focus on turnkey offerings, where procurement incentives reward rapid, standardized deployment while externalizing adaptation costs to clinicians. The study extends work-design and sociotechnical theory by locating job design in upstream productization and not only in organizational implementation. It also reframes debates on workplace automation by linking market incentives to patterned consequences for work. We conclude with implications for procurement, regulation, and participatory co-design.

session_name: Technological Change at Work and Across Industries
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Hye Jin Rho (Michigan State University), Christine A. Riordan (University of Illinois)
author_names: Rho, Hye Jin*; Riordan, Christine A.
title: From Rhythms to Stop, Drop, and Roll: Unpacking the Impact of Algorithmic Management on Discretion in Hotel Housekeeping Work
abstract: A key concern regarding the spread of algorithmic management (AM) beyond gig work is how it reshapes workers' discretion, or latitude to make decisions. When overlaid onto pre-existing routines, AM introduces temporal volatility by dynamically sequencing tasks, allocating assignments, and adjusting pacing in real time. How do such transformations affect workers' discretion over rhythms of work, and how do they respond? Drawing on a qualitative study of hotel housekeeping, the authors show that guest room attendants exercise meaningful discretion over their work, relying on contextualized and embodied knowledge to sequence rooms, adjust pacing, and manage physical effort. AM disrupts these practices by curtailing sequencing and creating pressure, through interruptions, while cleaning rooms. Yet workers actively rebuild temporal structures through "rhythmic reconstitution," blending algorithmic directives with situated knowledge, improvisation, and negotiation. We further evaluate these qualitative findings using an original, recently completed national survey of guest room attendants. Together, the findings reveal how AM transforms discretion over rhythms, advancing studies of technology, the labor process, and temporality in organizations.

session_name: Technological Change at Work and Across Industries
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Alexander Kowalski (Cornell University), Shruti Appalla (Cornell University)
title: 'Two Snakes with One Head:' How Automation Creates Relational Cleavages between Interdependent Work Groups
abstract: Even the most advanced technologies typically automate only portions of a work process, rather than the process in its entirety. This "modularization" creates divisions between workers directly affected by automation and those who share the same workspace but perform jobs that have not been so transformed, potentially altering relationships between these two groups. Through a comparative analysis of six e-commerce fulfillment centers, we examine the extent to which partial automation creates tensions between interdependent work groups. We compare functionally equivalent jobs across facilities that use one of three main technologies to complete the same work process: collaborative robots, conveyors, or hand-pulled carts. With field observations and more than 100 interviews, we show that the partial automation that results when robotics are introduced to only select roles creates "automation cleavages"—fault lines between groups that work with the robots and those that do not. Four dimensions of negative differentiation emerge at these boundaries: robotics workers are perceived by their coworkers in other roles as unreliable (blamed for technology malfunctions), unavailable (physically isolated and socially inaccessible), unalike (having different workplace values and levels of organizational commitment), and unworthy (performing easier work requiring less effort). These divisions undermine collaboration and coordination, resulting in slower production, extended downtimes, and decreased workforce satisfaction. The findings challenge optimistic predictions about collaborative robots improving job quality. Instead, partial automation erects social barriers between workers of similar status, producing relational inequalities between automation "haves" and "have-nots" within shared workspaces. Our study contributes to understanding how intelligent technologies transform workplace social relations, extending the work design literature and highlighting the unintended organizational consequences of technological modularization.

session_name: Technological Change at Work and Across Industries
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Sean O'Brady (McMaster University), Jeonghun Kim (Cornell University)
title: Contested Automation: Double Indeterminacies, Job Quality, and Union Resistance in Call Centers
abstract: This article analyzes how unions resist the harmful effects of automating technologies on working conditions. Drawing on semi-structured interviews, workshops, and survey data gathered from Canadian and U.S. call centers, it examines union contestation over the effects of self-service "job-replacing" technologies, e.g., self-order forms, chatbots, and interactive voice recognition systems. Building on Smith's conceptualization of "double indeterminacies" within the labor process, we argue that work effort and mobility represent two main domains of contestation over the deployment of automating technologies. The findings show how automation threatens working conditions across both indeterminacies. On the one hand, automation increases work effort by creating errors that must be handled by agents and by subordinating workers to mandated protocols. On the other hand, automation weakens workers' mobility power and job security by making them more replaceable, as it takes over customer inquiries. In response to these changes, unions' collective bargaining provisions for job security protect workers from layoff threats due to automation, while disciplinary and monitoring provisions reduce work intensity arising from work process disruptions. The current article makes two significant contributions. First, we extend the concept of double indeterminacies to understand the impact of emerging automation technologies. By extending this framework, we add greater theoretical precision to analyses of how technologies shape work across two domains. Second, we show how unions' collective bargaining comes into play in the "social shaping of technologies." Specifically, the article highlights that the institutional legacy of past struggles remains effective in protecting workers from harms associated with new technologies.

session_name: Taking Stock: System Dynamics Modeling in Industry Studies
title: Managing Capacity for Electric Vehicle Batteries Recycling
abstract: Recycling electric vehicle (EV) batteries is essential for reducing reliance on virgin raw materials, and proper planning of recycling capacity is necessary. Recycling facilities rely on two main sources of feedstock – used batteries from retired EVs and production scrap from manufacturing of batteries for new EVs. Currently, due to the limited installed base of EVs, the supply of used batteries is low, but is expected to increase as more EVs are sold. Conversely, production scrap is currently high but is bound to decrease within the next few years as manufacturing processes mature. Balancing these two trends is important to maintain sufficient recycling capacity and its efficient utilization. Although optimistic EV sales projections created significant expansion of battery production and recycling facilities in the last few years, recent consumer hesitancy and announcements from OEMs to slow or pause EV production suggest a substantially lower EV sales growth trajectory vs. earlier estimates. Consequently, not only EV battery production may experience an "overshoot-and-collapse" dynamic, but future flows of used EV batteries will decrease, leading to periods of underutilized recycling capacity and reduced demand for recycled materials. We use a fully calibrated model of the U.S. vehicle fleet to explore the feedback between trajectories of EV sales, EV battery production, and recycling capacity, focusing on optimal recycling capacity planning. Our findings offer strategic insights for vehicle OEMs, battery manufacturers, and recyclers to establish robust and resilient operational policies for EV battery recycling.

session_name: Taking Stock: System Dynamics Modeling in Industry Studies
authors: Edward Anderson (University of Texas at Austin), Sergey Naumov (Pennsylvania State University), Burcu Tan (University of New Mexico), Robert Benny (University of Texas at Austin)
author_names: Anderson, Edward*; Naumov, Sergey; Tan, Burcu; Benny, Robert
title: Cartels, Policy, and Technological Substitution: What the history of the Synthetic Rubber Industry Can Teach Us About the Rare Earths Supply Chain
abstract: Rare earth elements are critical inputs to sustainability, defense, and a wide range of other advanced technologies, yet their supply chains remain highly concentrated and vulnerable to disruption. In this presentation, we draw lessons from the twentieth-century history of the U.S. synthetic rubber industry to illuminate the dynamics shaping contemporary rare earth supply chains. Revisiting the longer arc of synthetic rubber development, we use a system dynamics approach to show how cartel power, policy intervention, and technological substitution repeatedly interacted to produce cycles of supply restriction, capacity expansion, and innovation. We then examine how these historical dynamics map onto today's rare earth supply chains and the policy challenges they pose. Concentrated processing capacity controlled by regional cartels, together with growing industry interest in reshoring capacity, material substitution, and design-based workarounds, closely mirrors the forces observed in the rubber industry. U.S. policy interventions can support industry efforts to reduce dependence on cartel power across the rare earth supply chain—from extraction and refining to midstream products such as permanent magnets. At the same time, cartel-controlled suppliers may act strategically to deter or undermine private investment, further complicating policy responses and underscoring the need for adaptive, evolving policy approaches. We conclude by discussing implications for theory, managerial decision-making, and public policy in this critical domain.

session_name: Taking Stock: System Dynamics Modeling in Industry Studies
authors: Alexander Kuptel (MIT Sloan School of Management), John Sterman (MIT Sloan School of Management)
title: Doubling Down on Dual-Fuels: Heat Pump and Fossil Backups' Effects on Grid Load, Cost, and Emissions in Massachusetts
abstract: Heat pumps (HPs) are a key technology to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and many governments offer HP rebates funded by utility ratepayers. However, rising electricity bills increase pressure to reduce rebates, and adoption may exacerbate winter peak electricity demand when HPs are least efficient. Dual-fuel systems are one proposed solution: they usually utilize a heat pump but use a fossil fuel backup in cold periods, lowering grid load. Moreover, heat pumps in these systems can have less capacity, limiting installation costs and allowing for lower rebates. We develop a system dynamics model of heating system purchases. The model distinguishes between homeowners replacing a broken system or reconsidering a functioning one. Homeowners consider both operating and installation costs, and those with functioning systems can retain them as backups to limit dual-fuels' incremental costs. The model is calibrated to Massachusetts, a cold-climate state with ambitious HP adoption targets. We find rebates for dual-fuel systems reduce peak load but increase emissions and subsidy outlays. Because homeowners can keep existing systems as backups, dual-fuels are popular with low rebates and increasing subsidies causes nearly all HPs to be dual-fuels, raising outlays and emissions from backups. Conversely, shifting rebate levels to all-electric systems lowers emissions with minimal change in outlays – but raises peak demand. Our results suggest limiting rebates for dual-fuel systems and complementing all-electric HP rebates with demand-side policies, such as energy efficiency incentives. More broadly, our work highlights that installed base effects can amplify the unintended fiscal and environmental consequences of technology subsidies.
